toolUseResult.originalFile:
Our evaluation covers three datasets but only one RE benchmark (SciERC), where 40\% of instances receive zero F1, compressing the discriminable range and limiting signal differentiation for relation extraction.
RE selection failure persists even when restricting to non-zero F1 instances (Appendix~\ref{app:re_conditional_selection}), ruling out floor effects as the sole explanation, but generalization to other RE benchmarks remains unvalidated.
WNUT-17 confirms the capability boundary of our approach, but our positive results on formal-domain text (CoNLL, SciERC) have not been validated on informal or noisy text where models achieve non-trivial performance.

We evaluate two model families (Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B), both at 8B parameters.
A 3-seed robustness analysis confirms that signal rankings are stable across seeds ($\sigma{\leq}0.026$; Table~\ref{tab:multiseed}), but whether our findings---particularly the correlation-selection gap and the difficulty-dependent signal ordering---hold for larger models (70B+) or closed-source APIs remains untested.
Larger models may produce higher-quality and more diverse samples, potentially altering the signal landscape.

Our analysis of selection potential uses only unsupervised signals.
We do not train a dedicated verifier or reward model, leaving unknown how much of the oracle headroom a supervised approach could recover.

We evaluate at $N{=}8$ and $N{=}16$.
The behavior of confidence signals at larger sample sizes (e.g., $N{=}64$ or $N{=}128$) is unknown, and $N$-scaling gains are setting-dependent: SJ improves by $+0.047$ on Qwen SciERC NER but only $+0.016$ on LLaMA SciERC NER when doubling from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$.

On CoNLL with LLaMA, the SJ--FK gap is only 0.003 ($\rho{=}0.431$ vs.\ $0.428$), so the structural advantage over surface signals may not generalize to all simple-schema datasets.
Our free-form ablation (\S\ref{sec:ablation}) confirms that LP score compression persists without constrained decoding, but was conducted on a single dataset (SciERC) with one model (Qwen3-8B); whether the compression finding generalizes to other datasets, model families, or model scales remains untested.

Qwen3-8B's SciERC checkpoint was trained with \texttt{enable\_thinking} active, injecting empty \texttt{<think></think>} blocks (4--5 tokens, no reasoning chain) before each response; CoNLL and WNUT checkpoints disabled this feature.
At inference time, constrained decoding suppresses thinking tokens in all configurations, so they do not appear in generated samples.
The empty blocks may weakly affect first-token probability distributions during training, potentially shifting LP score calibration on SciERC; however, since LP selection fails across all datasets including CoNLL and WNUT-17 (which lack this confound), the thinking token inconsistency is unlikely to explain the correlation-selection gap.
The absence of any reasoning content further limits the representational impact.

Finally, log-probability was excluded from the temperature comparison ($T{=}0.7$ vs.\ $T{=}1.0$) due to missing $T{=}0.7$ LP data; all LP compression analyses use $T{=}1.0$ exclusively, and whether compression behavior changes at lower temperatures remains unknown.
The free-form ablation (within-instance std ratio $0.97{\times}$) provides stronger evidence that compression is not an artifact of the decoding strategy, but does not address temperature as a variable.
Since practitioners commonly deploy at $T{<}1.0$ for reliability, this untested dependence represents a gap between our evaluation conditions ($T{=}1.0$) and typical deployment settings.
Lower temperatures concentrate probability mass on fewer tokens, which could either reduce LP compression (by widening score gaps between high- and low-probability sequences) or exacerbate it (by collapsing diversity so that all $N$ samples share near-identical token-level likelihoods).
The direction of this interaction is not predictable from first principles and depends on how the model's likelihood surface interacts with the structured output space.
Resolving this would require a controlled $T$-sweep with LP data at each temperature, which our experimental pipeline did not collect.

The absence of any reasoning content further limits the representational impact.

+One of three seeds (seed${=}456$) was run with \texttt{--subtask joint} (joint NER+RE decoding) rather than \texttt{--subtask ner} used by the other two seeds; the resulting NER F1 difference is ${<}0.3$~pp and falls within normal seed variance, so we retain this seed in 3-seed analyses without correction.

\begin{abstract}
Test-time scaling through repeated sampling promises quality gains for LLM-based information extraction, but whether confidence signals can identify the best output among multiple candidates remains untested for structured tasks.
Under constrained decoding---the standard regime for schema-compliant IE---we evaluate five confidence signals from three families across NER and relation extraction on three benchmarks with two 8B-parameter model families.
These signals achieve strong quality estimation, yet none significantly improves sample selection over greedy decoding despite 13--18 percentage points of oracle headroom.
Four of five signals are instance-level by construction and cannot rank candidates; the key empirical question is whether log-probability---the sole per-sample signal---or consensus-proximity selection can bridge this gap.
Neither succeeds: log-probability scores are compressed into effective ties for 60\% of instances under constrained decoding, while consensus-proximity (MBR decoding) fails because utility correlates with quality across instances but not within them.
Where log-probability compression is absent, selection recovers significant gains ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$), identifying constrained-decoding score compression as the primary bottleneck.
Signal rankings further depend on task complexity, with findings consistent across model families.
\end{abstract}

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Practical recommendations.}
For per-instance quality ranking, VC provides the strongest rank correlation ($\rho{=}0.38$), though EM leads binary discrimination (AUROC${=}0.749$); under conditional filtering, EM leads on both NER and RE ($\rho{=}0.360$, $0.417$; RE: preliminary, single benchmark).
Signal rankings depend on task difficulty---EM dominates easy tasks (CoNLL), VC and SJ dominate hard tasks (SciERC)---directionally consistent across two model families at 8B scale, though with model-dependent magnitude.
At higher sample sizes ($N{=}16$), SJ converges to comparable NER performance with VC ($\Delta{=}0.002$) with lower cross-seed variance ($\sigma{=}0.010$ vs.\ $0.026$); on RE, only VC consistently outperforms LP (preliminary).
When model capability is insufficient (WNUT-17), all signals converge toward non-significant conditional correlations (Table~\ref{tab:wnut}).

\paragraph{Why the gap exists: two layers.}
\textit{Layer 1 (definitional):} Four of five signals are instance-level aggregates that assign a single score per input; they cannot rank candidates by construction.
Consensus-proximity selection (\S\ref{sec:evaluation}) does not recover per-sample discrimination (Table~\ref{tab:selection}).
\textit{Layer 2 (score compression):} Log-probability, the only per-sample signal, also fails to exploit the 12--18~pp oracle headroom.
LP scores are severely compressed: the median within-instance LP range is only 0.041 nats, below the $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ threshold at which 60\% of instances are effectively tied, and 75\% of pairwise comparisons fall within $|\Delta|{<}0.026$ (Appendix~\ref{app:logprob_ties}).
In the 40\% of instances where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), LP \textit{significantly} outperforms greedy ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$; within-instance $\rho$: 0.08$\to$0.39).
This diagnostic confirms that LP carries useful per-sample quality information; score compression is the primary mechanistic bottleneck.
A controlled NER ablation (\S\ref{sec:ablation}) confirms that LP compression persists without constrained decoding; on RE, the interaction is task-dependent.
Diversity-stratified analysis confirms the gap persists even among high-diversity instances (Appendix~\ref{app:diversity}); RE miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339, preliminary; Appendix~\ref{app:calibration}) may compound this.

\paragraph{The gap widens with $N$.}
Doubling from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$ expands oracle headroom from 12.5 to 16.9~pp ($+4.4$~pp), yet signal-based selection fails to capture this growth.
LP, the best signal, improves by only $+0.4$~pp ($\Delta$: $+0.0{\to}+0.5$~pp), leaving 16.4~pp of headroom unrealized---a 31\% expansion of the gap.
VC deteriorates further ($\Delta$: $-2.5{\to}{-}3.1$~pp), a counterintuitive result for majority voting: with more candidates, systematic errors in entity-level frequency counts dominate, amplifying selection bias rather than correcting it.
This scaling behavior confirms that the correlation-selection gap is not a small-$N$ artifact; unsupervised signals face a structural ceiling that widens as oracle headroom grows.

\paragraph{Connection to MBR decoding.}
Our selection strategies instantiate minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, muller2021understanding}: each selects $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} U(y_i, y_j)$ with utility $U$ defined by SJ, EM, or entity overlap.
Despite MBR's success in machine translation \cite{freitag2022high} and its extension to summarization, code generation, and captioning \cite{jinnai2024mbr}, all variants fail here because the utility functions correlate with F1 at the instance level but not within a single instance---the mathematical essence of the correlation-selection gap.
\citet{eikema2025structured} study structure-conditional MBR decoding and find that standard utility functions degrade on structured outputs---consistent with our finding that consensus-proximity selection fails in IE despite its success in machine translation.

\paragraph{Score compression under free-form decoding.}\label{sec:ablation}
A natural hypothesis is that LP compression is an artifact of constrained decoding's restricted token space.
We test this via controlled ablation on SciERC (Qwen3-8B, single dataset): generating free-form (unconstrained) outputs on the same instances with post-hoc JSON parsing (parse rate 99.95\%, 4406/4408; Table~\ref{tab:freeform_ablation}).
For NER, LP variance is essentially unchanged (within-instance std ratio $0.97{\times}$, tied fraction 59.7\%$\to$57.7\%) and selection gains remain negligible ($+0.18$~pp free-form vs.\ $+0.59$~pp constrained), establishing that NER LP compression persists independent of decoding regime in our setting.
However, the ablation reveals a task-dependent interaction: RE LP selection flips from $-0.68$~pp (constrained) to $+1.69$~pp (free-form; preliminary, single seed).
This reversal falls within the NER bootstrap 95\% CI [$-3.0$, $+4.2$]~pp and is based on a single seed, so we do not treat it as a confirmed finding; it suggests that constrained decoding may interact differently with RE but requires multi-seed replication.
The NER/RE divergence indicates that the relationship between decoding regime and selection is task-specific in our setting.
Notably, the fine-tuned model achieved 99.95\% parse rate without grammar constraints, suggesting that constrained decoding's format-compliance role may be redundant for sufficiently fine-tuned models.

\paragraph{Task-specific decoding interactions.}
The free-form ablation reveals divergent behavior across tasks.
On RE, LP selection flips from $-0.68$~pp (constrained) to $+1.69$~pp (free-form; preliminary, single RE benchmark), a reversal that spans all 7 relation types and is driven by selective variance reallocation ($p{<}0.0001$).
The win/loss ratio shifts from 36:59 (constrained) to 45:45 (free-form), with the gains concentrated on relation-dense instances (mean 3.3 gold relations).
This interaction does not generalize to NER, where selection remains negligible under both regimes.
This ablation uses a single seed (seed${=}42$); whether the RE reversal replicates across seeds and generalizes to other RE benchmarks warrants further investigation.
Second, the non-tied subset ($n{=}210$) is partially reshuffled under free-form decoding: Jaccard similarity between the constrained and free-form non-tied sets is 0.472, indicating that 87 instances newly gain LP discrimination while others lose it, yielding a $3{\times}$ increase in within-instance LP range for the newly non-tied subset.
Despite this reshuffling, aggregate NER selection gains remain negligible---score compression is not a fixed property of specific instances but rather a pervasive regime that shifts across instances without producing net selection improvement.
Free-form decoding also slightly improves quality estimation (NER VC $\rho$: 0.379$\to$0.409), though this does not translate to selection gains.

\paragraph{Methodological implications.}
The decoupling of quality estimation ($\rho$), binary discrimination (AUROC), and sample selection (best-of-$N$ F1) means evaluating on a single metric risks selecting the wrong signal for the intended use case.
Effective selection likely requires per-sample signals such as trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}; $N$-scaling analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}) shows $N{=}8$ captures most quality estimation benefit.
Cross-dataset evaluation confirms that structural signals are robust to domain shift when the training schema subsumes the target (VC $\rho{=}0.469$ OOD vs.\ $0.379$ in-domain); the reverse direction fails due to catastrophic model failure, not signal failure (Appendix~\ref{app:ood}).
Our findings are established under constrained decoding at 8B scale; a single-dataset NER ablation suggests LP compression persists without constrained decoding, but RE shows task-dependent interaction with decoding regime.
Whether these patterns generalize across datasets, model scales, and decoding strategies warrants further investigation.

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Practical recommendations.}
For per-instance quality ranking, VC provides the strongest rank correlation ($\rho{=}0.38$), though EM leads binary discrimination (AUROC${=}0.749$); under conditional filtering, EM leads on both NER and RE ($\rho{=}0.360$, $0.417$; RE: preliminary, single benchmark).
Signal rankings depend on task difficulty---EM dominates easy tasks (CoNLL), VC and SJ dominate hard tasks (SciERC)---directionally consistent across two model families at 8B scale, though with model-dependent magnitude.
At higher sample sizes ($N{=}16$), SJ converges to comparable NER performance with VC ($\Delta{=}0.002$) with lower cross-seed variance ($\sigma{=}0.010$ vs.\ $0.026$); on RE, only VC consistently outperforms LP (preliminary).
When model capability is insufficient (WNUT-17), all signals converge toward non-significant conditional correlations (Table~\ref{tab:wnut}).

\paragraph{Why the gap exists: two layers.}
\textit{Layer 1 (definitional):} Four of five signals are instance-level aggregates that assign a single score per input; they cannot rank candidates by construction.
Consensus-proximity selection (\S\ref{sec:evaluation}) does not recover per-sample discrimination (Table~\ref{tab:selection}).
\textit{Layer 2 (score compression):} Log-probability, the only per-sample signal, also fails to exploit the 12--18~pp oracle headroom.
LP scores are severely compressed: the median within-instance LP range is only 0.041 nats, below the $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ threshold at which 60\% of instances are effectively tied, and 75\% of pairwise comparisons fall within $|\Delta|{<}0.026$ (Appendix~\ref{app:logprob_ties}).
In the 40\% of instances where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), LP \textit{significantly} outperforms greedy ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$; within-instance $\rho$: 0.08$\to$0.39).
This diagnostic confirms that LP carries useful per-sample quality information; score compression is the primary mechanistic bottleneck.
A controlled NER ablation (\S\ref{sec:ablation}) confirms that LP compression persists without constrained decoding; on RE, the interaction is task-dependent.
Diversity-stratified analysis confirms the gap persists even among high-diversity instances (Appendix~\ref{app:diversity}); RE miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339, preliminary; Appendix~\ref{app:calibration}) may compound this.

\paragraph{The gap widens with $N$.}
Doubling from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$ expands oracle headroom from 12.5 to 16.9~pp ($+4.4$~pp), yet signal-based selection fails to capture this growth.
LP, the best signal, improves by only $+0.4$~pp ($\Delta$: $+0.0{\to}+0.5$~pp), leaving 16.4~pp of headroom unrealized---a 31\% expansion of the gap.
VC deteriorates further ($\Delta$: $-2.5{\to}{-}3.1$~pp), a counterintuitive result for majority voting: with more candidates, systematic errors in entity-level frequency counts dominate, amplifying selection bias rather than correcting it.
On RE at $N{=}16$ (3-seed), the pattern is even more severe: oracle headroom reaches 17.1~pp, yet no signal matches the greedy baseline (best: VC $\Delta{=}{-}0.8$~pp, $p{\approx}0.8$; preliminary).
This scaling behavior confirms that the correlation-selection gap is not a small-$N$ artifact; unsupervised signals face a structural ceiling that widens as oracle headroom grows.

\paragraph{Connection to MBR decoding.}
Our selection strategies instantiate minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, muller2021understanding}: each selects $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} U(y_i, y_j)$ with utility $U$ defined by SJ, EM, or entity overlap.
Despite MBR's success in machine translation \cite{freitag2022high} and its extension to summarization, code generation, and captioning \cite{jinnai2024mbr}, all variants fail here because the utility functions correlate with F1 at the instance level but not within a single instance---the mathematical essence of the correlation-selection gap.
\citet{eikema2025structured} study structure-conditional MBR decoding and find that standard utility functions degrade on structured outputs---consistent with our finding that consensus-proximity selection fails in IE despite its success in machine translation.

\paragraph{Score compression under free-form decoding.}\label{sec:ablation}
A natural hypothesis is that LP compression is an artifact of constrained decoding's restricted token space.
We test this via controlled ablation on SciERC (Qwen3-8B, single dataset): generating free-form (unconstrained) outputs on the same instances with post-hoc JSON parsing (parse rate 99.95\%, 4406/4408; Table~\ref{tab:freeform_ablation}).
For NER, LP variance is essentially unchanged (within-instance std ratio $0.97{\times}$, tied fraction 59.7\%$\to$57.7\%) and selection gains remain negligible ($+0.18$~pp free-form vs.\ $+0.59$~pp constrained), establishing that NER LP compression persists independent of decoding regime in our setting.
However, the ablation reveals a task-dependent interaction: RE LP selection flips from $-0.68$~pp (constrained) to $+1.69$~pp (free-form; preliminary, single seed).
This reversal falls within the NER bootstrap 95\% CI [$-3.0$, $+4.2$]~pp and is based on a single seed, so we do not treat it as a confirmed finding; it suggests that constrained decoding may interact differently with RE but requires multi-seed replication.
The NER/RE divergence indicates that the relationship between decoding regime and selection is task-specific in our setting.
Notably, the fine-tuned model achieved 99.95\% parse rate without grammar constraints, suggesting that constrained decoding's format-compliance role may be redundant for sufficiently fine-tuned models.

\paragraph{Task-specific decoding interactions.}
The free-form ablation reveals divergent behavior across tasks.
On RE, LP selection flips from $-0.68$~pp (constrained) to $+1.69$~pp (free-form; preliminary, single RE benchmark), a reversal that spans all 7 relation types and is driven by selective variance reallocation ($p{<}0.0001$).
The win/loss ratio shifts from 36:59 (constrained) to 45:45 (free-form), with the gains concentrated on relation-dense instances (mean 3.3 gold relations).
This interaction does not generalize to NER, where selection remains negligible under both regimes.
This ablation uses a single seed (seed${=}42$); whether the RE reversal replicates across seeds and generalizes to other RE benchmarks warrants further investigation.
Second, the non-tied subset ($n{=}210$) is partially reshuffled under free-form decoding: Jaccard similarity between the constrained and free-form non-tied sets is 0.472, indicating that 87 instances newly gain LP discrimination while others lose it, yielding a $3{\times}$ increase in within-instance LP range for the newly non-tied subset.
Despite this reshuffling, aggregate NER selection gains remain negligible---score compression is not a fixed property of specific instances but rather a pervasive regime that shifts across instances without producing net selection improvement.
Free-form decoding also slightly improves quality estimation (NER VC $\rho$: 0.379$\to$0.409), though this does not translate to selection gains.

\paragraph{Methodological implications.}
The decoupling of quality estimation ($\rho$), binary discrimination (AUROC), and sample selection (best-of-$N$ F1) means evaluating on a single metric risks selecting the wrong signal for the intended use case.
Effective selection likely requires per-sample signals such as trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}; $N$-scaling analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}) shows $N{=}8$ captures most quality estimation benefit.
Cross-dataset evaluation confirms that structural signals are robust to domain shift when the training schema subsumes the target (VC $\rho{=}0.469$ OOD vs.\ $0.379$ in-domain); the reverse direction fails due to catastrophic model failure, not signal failure (Appendix~\ref{app:ood}).
Our findings are established under constrained decoding at 8B scale; a single-dataset NER ablation suggests LP compression persists without constrained decoding, but RE shows task-dependent interaction with decoding regime.
Whether these patterns generalize across datasets, model scales, and decoding strategies warrants further investigation.

\begin{abstract}
Test-time scaling through repeated sampling promises quality gains for LLM-based information extraction, but whether confidence signals can identify the best output among multiple candidates remains untested for structured tasks.
Under constrained decoding---the standard regime for schema-compliant IE---we evaluate five confidence signals from three families across NER and relation extraction on three benchmarks with two 8B-parameter model families.
These signals achieve strong quality estimation, yet none significantly improves sample selection over greedy decoding despite 13--18 percentage points of oracle headroom.
Four of five signals are instance-level by construction and cannot rank candidates; the key empirical question is whether log-probability---the sole per-sample signal---or consensus-proximity selection can bridge this gap.
Neither succeeds: log-probability scores are compressed into effective ties for 60\% of instances under constrained decoding, while consensus-proximity (MBR decoding) fails because utility correlates with quality across instances but not within them.
Where log-probability compression is absent, selection recovers significant gains ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$), identifying constrained-decoding score compression as the primary bottleneck.
Signal rankings further depend on task complexity, with findings consistent across model families.
\end{abstract}

10	\textit{Layer 1 (definitional):} Four of five signals are instance-level aggregates that assign a single score per input; they cannot rank candidates by construction.
11	Consensus-proximity selection (\S\ref{sec:evaluation}) does not recover per-sample discrimination (Table~\ref{tab:selection}).
12	\textit{Layer 2 (score compression):} Log-probability, the only per-sample signal, also fails to exploit the 12--18~pp oracle headroom.
13	LP scores are severely compressed: the median within-instance LP range is only 0.041 nats, below the $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ threshold at which 60\% of instances are effectively tied, and 75\% of pairwise comparisons fall within $|\Delta|{<}0.026$ (Appendix~\ref{app:logprob_ties}).
14	In the 40\% of instances where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), LP \textit{significantly} outperforms greedy ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$; within-instance $\rho$: 0.08$\to$0.39).
15	This diagnostic confirms that LP carries useful per-sample quality information; score compression is the primary mechanistic bottleneck.
16	A controlled NER ablation (\S\ref{sec:ablation}) confirms that LP compression persists without constrained decoding; on RE, the interaction is task-dependent.
17	Diversity-stratified analysis confirms the gap persists even among high-diversity instances (Appendix~\ref{app:diversity}); RE miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339, preliminary; Appendix~\ref{app:calibration}) may compound this.
18	
19	\paragraph{The gap widens with $N$.}
20	Doubling from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$ expands oracle headroom from 12.5 to 16.9~pp ($+4.4$~pp), yet signal-based selection fails to capture this growth.
21	LP, the best signal, improves by only $+0.4$~pp ($\Delta$: $+0.0{\to}+0.5$~pp), leaving 16.4~pp of headroom unrealized---a 31\% expansion of the gap.
22	VC deteriorates further ($\Delta$: $-2.5{\to}{-}3.1$~pp), a counterintuitive result for majority voting: with more candidates, systematic errors in entity-level frequency counts dominate, amplifying selection bias rather than correcting it.
23	On RE at $N{=}16$ (3-seed), the pattern is even more severe: oracle headroom reaches 17.1~pp, yet no signal matches the greedy baseline (best: VC $\Delta{=}{-}0.8$~pp, $p{\approx}0.8$; preliminary).
24	This scaling behavior confirms that the correlation-selection gap is not a small-$N$ artifact; unsupervised signals face a structural ceiling that widens as oracle headroom grows.
25	
26	\paragraph{Connection to MBR decoding.}
27	Our selection strategies instantiate minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, muller2021understanding}: each selects $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} U(y_i, y_j)$ with utility $U$ defined by SJ, EM, or entity overlap.
28	Despite MBR's success in machine translation \cite{freitag2022high} and its extension to summarization, code generation, and captioning \cite{jinnai2024mbr}, all variants fail here because the utility functions correlate with F1 at the instance level but not within a single instance---the mathematical essence of the correlation-selection gap.
29	\citet{eikema2025structured} study structure-conditional MBR decoding and find that standard utility functions degrade on structured outputs---consistent with our finding that consensus-proximity selection fails in IE despite its success in machine translation.
30	
31	\paragraph{Score compression under free-form decoding.}\label{sec:ablation}
32	A natural hypothesis is that LP compression is an artifact of constrained decoding's restricted token space.
33	We test this via controlled ablation on SciERC (Qwen3-8B, single dataset): generating free-form (unconstrained) outputs on the same instances with post-hoc JSON parsing (parse rate 99.95\%, 4406/4408; Table~\ref{tab:freeform_ablation}).
34	For NER, LP variance is essentially unchanged (within-instance std ratio $0.97{\times}$, tied fraction 59.7\%$\to$57.7\%) and selection gains remain negligible ($+0.18$~pp free-form vs.\ $+0.59$~pp constrained), establishing that NER LP compression persists independent of decoding regime in our setting.
35	However, the ablation reveals a task-dependent interaction: RE LP selection flips from $-0.68$~pp (constrained) to $+1.69$~pp (free-form; preliminary, single seed).
36	This reversal falls within the NER bootstrap 95\% CI [$-3.0$, $+4.2$]~pp and is based on a single seed, so we do not treat it as a confirmed finding; it suggests that constrained decoding may interact differently with RE but requires multi-seed replication.
37	The NER/RE divergence indicates that the relationship between decoding regime and selection is task-specific in our setting.
38	Notably, the fine-tuned model achieved 99.95\% parse rate without grammar constraints, suggesting that constrained decoding's format-compliance role may be redundant for sufficiently fine-tuned models.
39	
40	\paragraph{Task-specific decoding interactions.}
41	The free-form ablation reveals divergent behavior across tasks.
42	On RE, LP selection flips from $-0.68$~pp (constrained) to $+1.69$~pp (free-form; preliminary, single RE benchmark), a reversal that spans all 7 relation types and is driven by selective variance reallocation ($p{<}0.0001$).
43	The win/loss ratio shifts from 36:59 (constrained) to 45:45 (free-form), with the gains concentrated on relation-dense instances (mean 3.3 gold relations).
44	This interaction does not generalize to NER, where selection remains negligible under both regimes.
45	This ablation uses a single seed (seed${=}42$); whether the RE reversal replicates across seeds and generalizes to other RE benchmarks warrants further investigation.
46	Second, the non-tied subset ($n{=}210$) is partially reshuffled under free-form decoding: Jaccard similarity between the constrained and free-form non-tied sets is 0.472, indicating that 87 instances newly gain LP discrimination while others lose it, yielding a $3{\times}$ increase in within-instance LP range for the newly non-tied subset.
47	Despite this reshuffling, aggregate NER selection gains remain negligible---score compression is not a fixed property of specific instances but rather a pervasive regime that shifts across instances without producing net selection improvement.
48	Free-form decoding also slightly improves quality estimation (NER VC $\rho$: 0.379$\to$0.409), though this does not translate to selection gains.
49	
50	\paragraph{Methodological implications.}
51	The decoupling of quality estimation ($\rho$), binary discrimination (AUROC), and sample selection (best-of-$N$ F1) means evaluating on a single metric risks selecting the wrong signal for the intended use case.
52	Effective selection likely requires per-sample signals such as trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}; $N$-scaling analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}) shows $N{=}8$ captures most quality estimation benefit.
53	Cross-dataset evaluation confirms that structural signals are robust to domain shift when the training schema subsumes the target (VC $\rho{=}0.469$ OOD vs.\ $0.379$ in-domain); the reverse direction fails due to catastrophic model failure, not signal failure (Appendix~\ref{app:ood}).
54	Our findings are established under constrained decoding at 8B scale; a single-dataset NER ablation suggests LP compression persists without constrained decoding, but RE shows task-dependent interaction with decoding regime.
55	Whether these patterns generalize across datasets, model scales, and decoding strategies warrants further investigation.
56

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Practical recommendations.}
For per-instance quality ranking, VC provides the strongest rank correlation ($\rho{=}0.38$), though EM leads binary discrimination (AUROC${=}0.749$); under conditional filtering, EM leads on both NER and RE ($\rho{=}0.360$, $0.417$; RE: preliminary, single benchmark).
Signal rankings depend on task difficulty---EM dominates easy tasks (CoNLL), VC and SJ dominate hard tasks (SciERC)---directionally consistent across two model families at 8B scale, though with model-dependent magnitude.
At higher sample sizes ($N{=}16$), SJ converges to comparable NER performance with VC ($\Delta{=}0.002$) with lower cross-seed variance ($\sigma{=}0.010$ vs.\ $0.026$); on RE, only VC consistently outperforms LP (preliminary).
When model capability is insufficient (WNUT-17), all signals converge toward non-significant conditional correlations (Table~\ref{tab:wnut}).

\paragraph{Why the gap exists: two layers.}
\textit{Layer 1 (definitional):} Four of five signals are instance-level aggregates that assign a single score per input; they cannot rank candidates by construction.
Consensus-proximity selection (\S\ref{sec:evaluation}) does not recover per-sample discrimination (Table~\ref{tab:selection}).
\textit{Layer 2 (score compression):} Log-probability, the only per-sample signal, also fails to exploit the 12--18~pp oracle headroom.
LP scores are severely compressed: the median within-instance LP range is only 0.041 nats, below the $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ threshold at which 60\% of instances are effectively tied, and 75\% of pairwise comparisons fall within $|\Delta|{<}0.026$ (Appendix~\ref{app:logprob_ties}).
In the 40\% of instances where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), LP \textit{significantly} outperforms greedy ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$; within-instance $\rho$: 0.08$\to$0.39).
This diagnostic confirms that LP carries useful per-sample quality information; score compression is the primary mechanistic bottleneck.
A controlled NER ablation (\S\ref{sec:ablation}) confirms that LP compression persists without constrained decoding; on RE, the interaction is task-dependent.
Diversity-stratified analysis confirms the gap persists even among high-diversity instances (Appendix~\ref{app:diversity}); RE miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339, preliminary; Appendix~\ref{app:calibration}) may compound this.

\paragraph{The gap widens with $N$.}
Doubling from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$ expands oracle headroom from 12.5 to 16.9~pp ($+4.4$~pp), yet signal-based selection fails to capture this growth.
LP, the best signal, improves by only $+0.4$~pp ($\Delta$: $+0.0{\to}+0.5$~pp), leaving 16.4~pp of headroom unrealized---a 31\% expansion of the gap.
VC deteriorates further ($\Delta$: $-2.5{\to}{-}3.1$~pp), a counterintuitive result for majority voting: with more candidates, systematic errors in entity-level frequency counts dominate, amplifying selection bias rather than correcting it.
On RE at $N{=}16$ (3-seed), the pattern is even more severe: oracle headroom reaches 17.1~pp, yet no signal matches the greedy baseline (best: VC $\Delta{=}{-}0.8$~pp, $p{\approx}0.8$; preliminary).
This scaling behavior confirms that the correlation-selection gap is not a small-$N$ artifact; unsupervised signals face a structural ceiling that widens as oracle headroom grows.

\paragraph{Connection to MBR decoding.}
Our selection strategies instantiate minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, muller2021understanding}: each selects $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} U(y_i, y_j)$ with utility $U$ defined by SJ, EM, or entity overlap.
Despite MBR's success in machine translation \cite{freitag2022high} and its extension to summarization, code generation, and captioning \cite{jinnai2024mbr}, all variants fail here because the utility functions correlate with F1 at the instance level but not within a single instance---the mathematical essence of the correlation-selection gap.
\citet{eikema2025structured} study structure-conditional MBR decoding and find that standard utility functions degrade on structured outputs---consistent with our finding that consensus-proximity selection fails in IE despite its success in machine translation.

\paragraph{Score compression under free-form decoding.}\label{sec:ablation}
A natural hypothesis is that LP compression is an artifact of constrained decoding's restricted token space.
We test this via controlled ablation on SciERC (Qwen3-8B, single dataset): generating free-form (unconstrained) outputs on the same instances with post-hoc JSON parsing (parse rate 99.95\%, 4406/4408; Table~\ref{tab:freeform_ablation}).
For NER, LP variance is essentially unchanged (within-instance std ratio $0.97{\times}$, tied fraction 59.7\%$\to$57.7\%) and selection gains remain negligible ($+0.18$~pp free-form vs.\ $+0.59$~pp constrained), establishing that NER LP compression persists independent of decoding regime in our setting.
However, the ablation reveals a task-dependent interaction: RE LP selection flips from $-0.68$~pp (constrained) to $+1.69$~pp (free-form; preliminary, single seed).
This reversal falls within the NER bootstrap 95\% CI [$-3.0$, $+4.2$]~pp and is based on a single seed, so we do not treat it as a confirmed finding; it suggests that constrained decoding may interact differently with RE but requires multi-seed replication.
The NER/RE divergence indicates that the relationship between decoding regime and selection is task-specific in our setting.
Notably, the fine-tuned model achieved 99.95\% parse rate without grammar constraints, suggesting that constrained decoding's format-compliance role may be redundant for sufficiently fine-tuned models.

\paragraph{Task-specific decoding interactions.}
The free-form ablation reveals divergent behavior across tasks.
On RE, LP selection flips from $-0.68$~pp (constrained) to $+1.69$~pp (free-form; preliminary, single RE benchmark), a reversal that spans all 7 relation types and is driven by selective variance reallocation ($p{<}0.0001$).
The win/loss ratio shifts from 36:59 (constrained) to 45:45 (free-form), with the gains concentrated on relation-dense instances (mean 3.3 gold relations).
This interaction does not generalize to NER, where selection remains negligible under both regimes.
This ablation uses a single seed (seed${=}42$); whether the RE reversal replicates across seeds and generalizes to other RE benchmarks warrants further investigation.
Second, the non-tied subset ($n{=}210$) is partially reshuffled under free-form decoding: Jaccard similarity between the constrained and free-form non-tied sets is 0.472, indicating that 87 instances newly gain LP discrimination while others lose it, yielding a $3{\times}$ increase in within-instance LP range for the newly non-tied subset.
Despite this reshuffling, aggregate NER selection gains remain negligible---score compression is not a fixed property of specific instances but rather a pervasive regime that shifts across instances without producing net selection improvement.
Free-form decoding also slightly improves quality estimation (NER VC $\rho$: 0.379$\to$0.409), though this does not translate to selection gains.

\paragraph{Methodological implications.}
The decoupling of quality estimation ($\rho$), binary discrimination (AUROC), and sample selection (best-of-$N$ F1) means evaluating on a single metric risks selecting the wrong signal for the intended use case.
Effective selection likely requires per-sample signals such as trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}; $N$-scaling analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}) shows $N{=}8$ captures most quality estimation benefit.
Cross-dataset evaluation confirms that structural signals are robust to domain shift when the training schema subsumes the target (VC $\rho{=}0.469$ OOD vs.\ $0.379$ in-domain); the reverse direction fails due to catastrophic model failure, not signal failure (Appendix~\ref{app:ood}).
Our findings are established under constrained decoding at 8B scale; a single-dataset NER ablation suggests LP compression persists without constrained decoding, but RE shows task-dependent interaction with decoding regime.
Whether these patterns generalize across datasets, model scales, and decoding strategies warrants further investigation.

103	\section{Additional Analyses}\label{app:additional}
104	
105	\paragraph{Per-relation diagnostic.}
106	RE signal degradation is relation-specific.
107	\textsc{Feature-Of} has near-zero correlation ($\rho{=}0.004$), while \textsc{Hyponym-Of} achieves $\rho{=}0.646$.
108	The primary bottleneck is entity span errors, which account for 55.5\% of RE false negatives---a prerequisite failure that consistency signals cannot detect, as they measure agreement among equally incorrect extractions.
109	We note that RE analysis relies on a single dataset (SciERC); generalization to other RE benchmarks remains to be validated.
110	
111	\paragraph{Capability stratification.}
112	For NER, SJ effectiveness scales with structural complexity: on SciERC instances with 6+ entities, $\rho{=}0.547$, compared to $\rho{=}0.415$ for 1--2 entities.
113	The SJ advantage over LP remains stable across sentence-length quartiles ($\Delta\rho{\approx}0.08$--$0.20$).
114	For RE, SJ $\rho$ increases monotonically with sentence length (Q1: 0.110 $\to$ Q4: 0.473; Fisher $z$-test $p{=}0.004$), indicating that longer, more relation-dense sentences provide richer structure for consistency-based estimation.
115	Both proxies are weakly correlated with F1 ($|r|{<}0.15$), confirming they capture input complexity rather than directly predicting output quality; however, entity count and sentence length are themselves moderately correlated ($\rho{=}0.650$), so they reflect overlapping rather than independent complexity dimensions.
116	For RE, entity count and relation count are strongly correlated ($\rho{=}0.769$) and thus reflect a single structural complexity dimension rather than independent axes.
117	On the high-complexity RE subset ($n{=}81$, high relation count), signals improve substantially: VC reaches $\rho{=}0.630$, LP $\rho{=}0.554$, and SJ $\rho{=}0.502$---all far above the full-set levels.
118	Richer relational structure provides more signal for consistency-based estimation, complementing the task-level boundary established by WNUT-17: structural signals are most effective within a ``sweet spot'' of sufficient model capability and sufficient output complexity.
119	
120	\paragraph{Length vs.\ log-probability.}
121	Figure~\ref{fig:length_logprob_scatter} shows that mean log-probability is weakly positively correlated with output length (NER: $\rho{=}0.386$, $n{=}4{,}232$; RE: $\rho{=}0.326$, $n{=}3{,}176$), ruling out length-penalty confounding as an explanation for LP's selection failure: longer outputs receive \textit{higher}, not lower, token-averaged log-probability under constrained decoding.
122	
123	\begin{figure}[t]
124	\centering
125	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig_length_logprob_scatter}
126	\caption{Output length vs.\ mean log-probability on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). Positive correlations (NER: $\rho{=}0.386$; RE: $\rho{=}0.326$) rule out length-penalty confounding.}
127	\label{fig:length_logprob_scatter}
128	\end{figure}
129	
130	\paragraph{Evaluation circularity and LOO-SJ equivalence.}
131	Consensus-proximity selection chooses $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$.
132	Leave-one-out SJ (LOO-SJ) for sample $y_i$ is $\text{LOO-SJ}_i = \frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$.
133	Since the $\frac{1}{N-1}$ constant is shared across all candidates within an instance, $\arg\max_{y_i} \text{LOO-SJ}_i = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$, making the two selection rules equivalent.
134	Standard (non-LOO) SJ adds the self-comparison term $\text{SJ}(y_i, y_i) = 1$ to each candidate, which is constant and thus does not affect ranking.
135	Empirically, LOO-SJ yields $\Delta\rho{=}{-}0.014$ relative to standard SJ (a correlation-level difference), with a maximum per-instance score difference of $3.1{\times}10^{-4}$ (negligible at the individual prediction level).
136	Evaluation circularity is negligible.
137	
138	\paragraph{Conditional filtering details.}
139	On LLaMA conditional RE (non-zero F1 instances), SJ recovers to $\rho{=}0.405$ while FK drops to $\rho{=}0.259$, consistent with the NER structural advantage; on full-set RE, however, the SJ--FK difference is non-significant ($\Delta\rho{=}{-}0.005$, $p{=}0.53$; preliminary).
140	At $N{=}16$, the divergence persists: SJ maintains $\rho{=}0.308$ on conditional RE while LP drops to $\rho{=}{-}0.026$.
141	EM ranks first across all four tested conditional configurations---SciERC NER ($\rho{=}0.360$), CoNLL Qwen $N{=}16$ ($\rho{=}0.466$), CoNLL LLaMA 3-seed ($\rho{=}0.462$), and SciERC RE ($\rho{=}0.417$)---despite full-set rankings ranging from \#1 (CoNLL Qwen) to \#5 (SciERC RE).
142	On the full set, EM is diluted by trivial agreement: instances where all $N$ samples produce identical (possibly incorrect) outputs receive EM${=}1$ regardless of quality, compressing the signal's dynamic range.
143	On the conditional set---where the model demonstrably produces varied outputs---exact agreement becomes the strongest quality signal.

192	\paragraph{Diminishing returns of $N$-scaling.}
193	Our $N{=}8$ and $N{=}16$ comparisons (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}) characterize the marginal value of additional samples for test-time scaling \cite{brown2024monkeys, snell2025scaling}.
194	For quality estimation, structural signals benefit consistently but sublinearly: SJ $\rho$ improves by $+0.047$ (Qwen SciERC, 3-seed mean) and $+0.032$ (LLaMA CoNLL, 3-seed mean) when doubling from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$, while log-probability is approximately $N$-invariant ($\Delta\rho{\leq}0.021$).
195	Structural signals leverage $\binom{N}{2}$ pairwise comparisons (28 pairs at $N{=}8$, 120 at $N{=}16$), but the $\rho$ improvement is far less than proportional, indicating diminishing information per additional comparison.
196	This asymmetry gives structural signals a relative advantage in the compute-constrained regime: at $N{=}8$, SJ already achieves $\rho{=}0.431$ on LLaMA CoNLL (vs.\ LP $\rho{=}0.307$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.124$), and the gap \textit{widens} at $N{=}16$ ($\Delta{=}{+}0.163$) because structural signals continue to benefit from additional pairwise evidence while LP does not.
197	For sample selection, additional samples increase the oracle upper bound---more draws raise the probability of a high-quality candidate---but signal-based selection remains flat because the selector's inability to identify the best candidate is a granularity limitation, not a sample size limitation.
198	The practical implication is that $N{=}8$ captures most of the achievable quality estimation benefit; further scaling widens rather than closes the correlation-selection gap absent stronger per-sample selectors.
199	
200	\paragraph{$N{=}16$ CoNLL selection: small but significant.}
201	While quality estimation benefits sublinearly from $N$-scaling, selection behavior at $N{=}16$ reveals a nuanced exception on LLaMA CoNLL.
202	VC achieves the largest gain over greedy ($+0.28$~pp, $p{=}0.003$--$0.027$ across 3 seeds, all significant), with SJ, FK, and EM at $+0.22$--$0.23$~pp and LP at $+0.12$~pp (2/3 seeds significant).
203	These gains are statistically significant but practically minimal: oracle headroom at $N{=}16$ is only 2.5~pp, so VC captures approximately 10\% of the available headroom.
204	This reinforces the primary finding: even under the most favorable conditions---high baseline performance, more candidates, and aggregated multi-seed evidence---signal-based selection recovers only a fraction of the oracle headroom available.

282	\paragraph{TOST equivalence testing.}

670	\paragraph{Wider-to-narrower schema transfer.}
671	When the SciERC-trained model (6 NER types) is applied to CoNLL (4 types), all signals remain significant ($p{<}0.001$) and structural signals improve over their in-domain levels (same model, seed${=}42$, $N{=}8$; in-domain $\rho$ from Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}): VC reaches $\rho{=}0.469$ (in-domain $0.379$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.090$), SJ $\rho{=}0.378$ (in-domain $0.360$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.018$), and FK $\rho{=}0.285$ (in-domain $0.267$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.018$).
672	The wider training schema subsumes CoNLL's narrower schema, so the model produces reasonable outputs even out-of-domain (greedy F1${=}0.522$), and structural signals benefit from the simpler target schema's reduced output ambiguity.
673	
674	\paragraph{Narrower-to-wider schema transfer (excluded).}
675	The reverse direction is excluded from our conclusions due to catastrophic model failure, not signal failure.
676	The CoNLL-trained model recognizes only 4 news entity types (PER, ORG, LOC, MISC) and has no relation extraction capability; when applied to SciERC's 6 scientific entity types and 7 relation types, the model cannot produce meaningful structured outputs (greedy NER F1${=}0.009$, RE F1${=}0.001$).

680	\paragraph{Asymmetry interpretation.}
681	The directional asymmetry is driven by schema coverage: wider$\to$narrower preserves signal utility because the SciERC model's 6-type schema subsumes CoNLL's 4 types, while narrower$\to$wider fails because the CoNLL model lacks the entity and relation types required by SciERC.
682	This extends the capability boundary identified on WNUT-17 to the domain-shift setting: confidence signals require sufficient model capability as a prerequisite, and results from the CoNLL$\to$SciERC direction should not be interpreted as evidence of signal degradation under domain shift.

\section{Robustness Analysis}\label{app:robustness}

For these instances, F1 is trivially zero regardless of prediction quality, and consistency signals reflect agreement on the empty set rather than extraction quality---including them inflates or deflates Spearman $\rho$ depending on signal behavior at the boundary.

\caption{Temperature robustness on SciERC ($N{=}8$). Top: NER; bottom: RE. SJ maintains stable $\rho$ across $T{=}0.7$ and $T{=}1.0$, while FK shows mixed sensitivity. LP $T{=}0.7$ data unavailable.}

\paragraph{Temperature sensitivity.}
SJ NER $\rho$ shifts from 0.388 ($T{=}0.7$) to 0.360 ($T{=}1.0$), a difference of 0.028 whose bootstrap confidence interval includes zero.
FK shows mixed behavior: NER $\rho$ drops by 0.054, while RE $\rho$ increases by 0.091, likely reflecting reduced diversity at lower temperature interacting differently across tasks.
Across all comparisons, the SJ--FK relative ordering is preserved at both temperatures on NER (0.388 vs.\ 0.321 at $T{=}0.7$; 0.360 vs.\ 0.267 at $T{=}1.0$), indicating a stable signal hierarchy despite numerically small temperature effects.

\paragraph{Sample size scaling.}
Increasing from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$ improves SJ on Qwen SciERC NER: $\rho$ rises from 0.360 to $0.411{\pm}0.010$ (three seeds: 0.398, 0.423, 0.410), a gain of $+0.047$.
The magnitude of $N$-scaling gains is setting-dependent---LLaMA SciERC NER yields $+0.016$ and Qwen CoNLL NER $+0.014$---though the direction is consistently positive.
LLaMA CoNLL exhibits the most uniform scaling: all four consistency signals gain $\Delta\rho{\approx}{+}0.030$ (range: $+0.027$ to $+0.032$) while LP gains only $+0.003$ (Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}).
FK $N$-scaling is inconsistent: degradation on SciERC ($-0.007$ to $-0.019$) but improvement on CoNLL with LLaMA ($+0.027$), suggesting sensitivity to both model and task characteristics.
VC $N$-scaling is consistently positive ($+0.005$ on Qwen CoNLL, $+0.018$ on LLaMA SciERC, $+0.030$ on Qwen SciERC), while LP is approximately $N$-invariant ($\Delta{\leq}0.034$).
SJ, EM, and VC scale consistently across all tested settings; only FK shows setting-dependent variation, suggesting that structural and binary-agreement signals are the most robust to $N$.
At $N{=}16$, SJ converges to comparable NER performance with VC ($\Delta{=}0.002$) while exhibiting lower cross-seed variance ($\sigma{=}0.010$ vs.\ $0.026$), making it a more stable alternative at higher sample sizes.

\paragraph{Transfer across model families.}
LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct shows a similar SJ--FK ordering on SciERC NER (SJ $\rho{=}0.325{\pm}0.021$, FK $\rho{=}0.256{\pm}0.024$, $\Delta\rho{=}0.069$; permutation $p{=}0.06$, borderline).
On CoNLL, the gap across model families is minimal (Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}): SJ achieves $\rho{=}0.431$ (LLaMA) vs.\ 0.436 (Qwen), $\Delta{=}0.005$.
At $N{=}16$, the structural-over-LP advantage holds across all four tested NER settings: Qwen SciERC (VC $\rho{=}0.409$ vs.\ LP 0.239, $\Delta{=}{+}0.170$), Qwen CoNLL (EM $\rho{=}0.463$ vs.\ LP 0.328, $\Delta{=}{+}0.135$), LLaMA SciERC (VC $\rho{=}0.452$ vs.\ LP 0.277, $\Delta{=}{+}0.175$), and LLaMA CoNLL 3-seed (SJ $\rho{=}0.476{\pm}0.006$ vs.\ LP $0.313{\pm}0.003$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.163$).

\section{Calibration Analysis}\label{app:calibration}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering

\caption{Reliability diagrams on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). Top: mean F1 vs.\ binned confidence; bottom: instance counts per bin. Left: NER; right: RE. NER signals are reasonably well-calibrated (calibration ECE 0.069--0.096), while RE shows greater miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339), reflecting the difficulty of calibrating confidence for compound extraction tasks.}
\label{fig:reliability}
\end{figure*}

Reliability diagrams use 10 equal-width bins.
NER signals are reasonably well-calibrated (calibration ECE 0.069--0.096), while RE exhibits greater miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339), indicating that translating consistency scores into calibrated confidence estimates is feasible for NER but remains challenging for compound extraction tasks.

\section{Additional Analyses}\label{app:additional}

\paragraph{Per-relation diagnostic.}
RE signal degradation is relation-specific.
\textsc{Feature-Of} has near-zero correlation ($\rho{=}0.004$), while \textsc{Hyponym-Of} achieves $\rho{=}0.646$.
The primary bottleneck is entity span errors, which account for 55.5\% of RE false negatives---a prerequisite failure that consistency signals cannot detect, as they measure agreement among equally incorrect extractions.
We note that RE analysis relies on a single dataset (SciERC); generalization to other RE benchmarks remains to be validated.

\paragraph{Capability stratification.}
For NER, SJ effectiveness scales with structural complexity: on SciERC instances with 6+ entities, $\rho{=}0.547$, compared to $\rho{=}0.415$ for 1--2 entities.
The SJ advantage over LP remains stable across sentence-length quartiles ($\Delta\rho{\approx}0.08$--$0.20$).
For RE, SJ $\rho$ increases monotonically with sentence length (Q1: 0.110 $\to$ Q4: 0.473; Fisher $z$-test $p{=}0.004$), indicating that longer, more relation-dense sentences provide richer structure for consistency-based estimation.
Both proxies are weakly correlated with F1 ($|r|{<}0.15$), confirming they capture input complexity rather than directly predicting output quality; however, entity count and sentence length are themselves moderately correlated ($\rho{=}0.650$), so they reflect overlapping rather than independent complexity dimensions.
For RE, entity count and relation count are strongly correlated ($\rho{=}0.769$) and thus reflect a single structural complexity dimension rather than independent axes.
On the high-complexity RE subset ($n{=}81$, high relation count), signals improve substantially: VC reaches $\rho{=}0.630$, LP $\rho{=}0.554$, and SJ $\rho{=}0.502$---all far above the full-set levels.
Richer relational structure provides more signal for consistency-based estimation, complementing the task-level boundary established by WNUT-17: structural signals are most effective within a ``sweet spot'' of sufficient model capability and sufficient output complexity.

\paragraph{Length vs.\ log-probability.}
Figure~\ref{fig:length_logprob_scatter} shows that mean log-probability is weakly positively correlated with output length (NER: $\rho{=}0.386$, $n{=}4{,}232$; RE: $\rho{=}0.326$, $n{=}3{,}176$), ruling out length-penalty confounding as an explanation for LP's selection failure: longer outputs receive \textit{higher}, not lower, token-averaged log-probability under constrained decoding.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig_length_logprob_scatter}
\caption{Output length vs.\ mean log-probability on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). Positive correlations (NER: $\rho{=}0.386$; RE: $\rho{=}0.326$) rule out length-penalty confounding.}
\label{fig:length_logprob_scatter}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Evaluation circularity and LOO-SJ equivalence.}
Consensus-proximity selection chooses $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$.
Leave-one-out SJ (LOO-SJ) for sample $y_i$ is $\text{LOO-SJ}_i = \frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$.
Since the $\frac{1}{N-1}$ constant is shared across all candidates within an instance, $\arg\max_{y_i} \text{LOO-SJ}_i = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$, making the two selection rules equivalent.
Standard (non-LOO) SJ adds the self-comparison term $\text{SJ}(y_i, y_i) = 1$ to each candidate, which is constant and thus does not affect ranking.
Empirically, LOO-SJ yields $\Delta\rho{=}{-}0.014$ relative to standard SJ (a correlation-level difference), with a maximum per-instance score difference of $3.1{\times}10^{-4}$ (negligible at the individual prediction level).
Evaluation circularity is negligible.

\paragraph{Conditional filtering details.}
On LLaMA conditional RE (non-zero F1 instances), SJ recovers to $\rho{=}0.405$ while FK drops to $\rho{=}0.259$, consistent with the NER structural advantage; on full-set RE, however, the SJ--FK difference is non-significant ($\Delta\rho{=}{-}0.005$, $p{=}0.53$; preliminary).
At $N{=}16$, the divergence persists: SJ maintains $\rho{=}0.308$ on conditional RE while LP drops to $\rho{=}{-}0.026$.
EM ranks first across all four tested conditional configurations---SciERC NER ($\rho{=}0.360$), CoNLL Qwen $N{=}16$ ($\rho{=}0.466$), CoNLL LLaMA 3-seed ($\rho{=}0.462$), and SciERC RE ($\rho{=}0.417$)---despite full-set rankings ranging from \#1 (CoNLL Qwen) to \#5 (SciERC RE).
On the full set, EM is diluted by trivial agreement: instances where all $N$ samples produce identical (possibly incorrect) outputs receive EM${=}1$ regardless of quality, compressing the signal's dynamic range.
On the conditional set---where the model demonstrably produces varied outputs---exact agreement becomes the strongest quality signal.
The margin over SJ is largest on RE ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.171$), where compound extraction decisions amplify output variability, and smallest on CoNLL LLaMA ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.002$), where all signals converge near $\rho{\approx}0.46$.

\paragraph{WNUT-17 full signal analysis.}
Table~\ref{tab:wnut} reports all five signals on WNUT-17.
VC achieves $\rho{=}0.724$ (AUROC${=}0.913$) on the full set, but conditional analysis (non-zero F1 instances) reveals this is entirely driven by the zero/non-zero boundary: conditional $\rho{=}0.038$ ($p{=}0.49$).
LP shows the reverse pattern: full-set $\rho{=}{-}0.410$ but conditional $\rho{=}0.350$, the highest among all signals on the conditional set.
This inversion confirms that full-set correlations on high-failure-rate datasets conflate binary success prediction with quality gradation.

\begin{table}[t]

\paragraph{Diminishing returns of $N$-scaling.}
Our $N{=}8$ and $N{=}16$ comparisons (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}) characterize the marginal value of additional samples for test-time scaling \cite{brown2024monkeys, snell2025scaling}.
For quality estimation, structural signals benefit consistently but sublinearly: SJ $\rho$ improves by $+0.047$ (Qwen SciERC, 3-seed mean) and $+0.032$ (LLaMA CoNLL, 3-seed mean) when doubling from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$, while log-probability is approximately $N$-invariant ($\Delta\rho{\leq}0.021$).
Structural signals leverage $\binom{N}{2}$ pairwise comparisons (28 pairs at $N{=}8$, 120 at $N{=}16$), but the $\rho$ improvement is far less than proportional, indicating diminishing information per additional comparison.
This asymmetry gives structural signals a relative advantage in the compute-constrained regime: at $N{=}8$, SJ already achieves $\rho{=}0.431$ on LLaMA CoNLL (vs.\ LP $\rho{=}0.307$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.124$), and the gap \textit{widens} at $N{=}16$ ($\Delta{=}{+}0.163$) because structural signals continue to benefit from additional pairwise evidence while LP does not.
For sample selection, additional samples increase the oracle upper bound---more draws raise the probability of a high-quality candidate---but signal-based selection remains flat because the selector's inability to identify the best candidate is a granularity limitation, not a sample size limitation.
The practical implication is that $N{=}8$ captures most of the achievable quality estimation benefit; further scaling widens rather than closes the correlation-selection gap absent stronger per-sample selectors.

\paragraph{$N{=}16$ CoNLL selection: small but significant.}
While quality estimation benefits sublinearly from $N$-scaling, selection behavior at $N{=}16$ reveals a nuanced exception on LLaMA CoNLL.
VC achieves the largest gain over greedy ($+0.28$~pp, $p{=}0.003$--$0.027$ across 3 seeds, all significant), with SJ, FK, and EM at $+0.22$--$0.23$~pp and LP at $+0.12$~pp (2/3 seeds significant).
These gains are statistically significant but practically minimal: oracle headroom at $N{=}16$ is only 2.5~pp, so VC captures approximately 10\% of the available headroom.
This reinforces the primary finding: even under the most favorable conditions---high baseline performance, more candidates, and aggregated multi-seed evidence---signal-based selection recovers only a fraction of the oracle headroom available.

\paragraph{Oracle-improvable fraction.}
Across SciERC configurations, 39--42\% of instances contain at least one sample with F1 exceeding greedy: Qwen NER 42.0\% (222/529, mean headroom $+$31.9~pp among improvable instances), Qwen RE 41.3\% (164/397, $+$45.3~pp), LLaMA NER 39.3\% (208/529, $+$33.7~pp).
On CoNLL, only 4--9\% of instances are improvable, confirming the ceiling effect.

\paragraph{Diversity-stratified selection gap.}
On the 44\% of Qwen SciERC instances with high diversity (${\geq}4$ unique outputs among 8 samples, $n{=}232$), oracle headroom reaches $+$16.3~pp, yet all consistency-based signals (SJ, FK, EM, VC) select at or below greedy, and LP---the only per-sample signal---achieves merely $+$0.8~pp.
LLaMA replicates this pattern: on its high-diversity subset ($n{=}186$), oracle headroom reaches $+$20.1~pp while consistency signals remain at or below greedy and LP captures only $+$2.0~pp.
This rules out insufficient diversity as an explanation for the correlation-selection gap.

\paragraph{TOST equivalence testing.}
The primary evidence against selection gains comes from effect sizes and confidence intervals: Cohen's $d{=}0.038$ for the best signal (NER LP) and bootstrap 95\% CI [$-$3.0, $+$4.2]~pp spanning zero.
Table~\ref{tab:tost} supplements this with two one-sided tests (TOST), testing whether each signal's selection F1 is equivalent to greedy within a bound $\delta$.
The $\delta$ values are contextualized against oracle headroom (12--18~pp): $\delta{=}5$~pp corresponds to forgoing 28--38\% of the available headroom, $\delta{=}3$~pp forgoing 17--23\%, and $\delta{=}2$~pp less than 15\%.
These proportions use the same test data that defines the headroom and should be interpreted as context for practical relevance rather than independent calibration.
The breakpoint $\delta^*$---the minimum equivalence margin at which each signal passes TOST---ranges from approximately 1.3~pp (SJ, ${\sim}$10\% of oracle headroom) to 3.4~pp (FK, ${\sim}$26\%) on NER, and from approximately 2.9~pp (LP, ${\sim}$16\%) to 6.5~pp (VC, ${\sim}$36\%) on RE.
On NER ($n{=}529$), at $\delta{=}{\pm}2$~pp, SJ and LP are confirmed equivalent to greedy (TOST $p{<}0.05$); at $\delta{=}{\pm}3$~pp, four of five signals pass; at $\delta{=}{\pm}5$~pp, all five pass.
On RE ($n{=}397$, preliminary), EM and VC fail equivalence even at $\delta{=}{\pm}5$~pp due to systematic underperformance ($\Delta{=}{-}3.2$~pp and $-4.5$~pp respectively).
The effect sizes are negligible ($d{=}0.038$) and confidence intervals span zero, with TOST confirming equivalence at practically meaningful margins.

\paragraph{Prompt template.}
For NER, we use a structured prompt:
\begin{quote}
\small
\texttt{System:} You are an expert in Named Entity Recognition.\\
\texttt{User:} Extract all named entities from the following text. Output as JSON.\\
Text: \texttt{\{input\_text\}}\\
Entity types: \texttt{\{schema\_types\}}
\end{quote}
RE follows the same structure with ``Relation Extraction'' and relation type lists substituted accordingly.

\paragraph{Constrained decoding.}
Inference uses vLLM with XGrammar-based JSON schema enforcement \cite{willard2023guided}, which constrains outputs to valid entity/relation structures matching the target schema.
This eliminates format errors but may compress per-sample diversity by restricting the output space.\footnote{SciERC training used \texttt{enable\_thinking=True} (LLaMA Factory 0.9.4 default), injecting empty \texttt{<think></think>} blocks (4--5 tokens) into each training response with loss computation; CoNLL and WNUT explicitly set \texttt{enable\_thinking=False}. Constrained decoding at inference time enforces JSON-only output, suppressing thinking tokens. See \S\ref{sec:setup} and Limitations for discussion of this confound.}

\section{Log-Probability Score Compression}\label{app:logprob_ties}

Under constrained decoding, log-probability scores are severely compressed within instances, limiting per-sample discrimination (Table~\ref{tab:logprob_ties}, Figure~\ref{fig:lp_range_cdf}).
The median within-instance LP range is only 0.041 nats---below the $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ threshold used throughout, providing data-driven justification for this cutoff rather than an arbitrary choice.
At $\varepsilon{=}0.05$, 60.3\% of instances ($n{=}529$, excluding empty gold annotations) have a within-sample range below the threshold, and 75\% of pairwise comparisons are effective ties ($|\Delta|{<}0.026$).
The CDF rises smoothly with no cliff or discontinuity (Figure~\ref{fig:lp_range_cdf}), confirming that compression is a pervasive regime rather than a bimodal split.
For comparison, SJ has only 12.5\% tied instances at the same threshold---SJ's advantage over LP for selection is one of score resolution, not information content.

\section{LP Selection Failure Stability}\label{app:lp_failure_stability}

We analyze RE LP selection failures across three random seeds (constrained decoding, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$, Qwen3-8B) to assess whether failures are systematic or stochastic.

\paragraph{Pairwise overlap.}
LP selection failures (instances where LP-selected F1 $<$ greedy F1) show moderate cross-seed stability: the average pairwise Jaccard similarity is 0.42 (range: 0.38--0.46), indicating that failures are partially systematic---driven by instance complexity---but not fully deterministic.
The 3-way intersection contains 34 instances (27.9\% of any-seed failures), confirming a stable failure core.

Failure rate increases monotonically with gold relation count: 4.3\% at 1 relation, 20.7\% at 3 relations, 26.2\% at 6 relations.

\paragraph{Wider-to-narrower schema transfer.}
When the SciERC-trained model (6 NER types) is applied to CoNLL (4 types), all signals remain significant ($p{<}0.001$) and structural signals improve over their in-domain levels (same model, seed${=}42$, $N{=}8$; in-domain $\rho$ from Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}): VC reaches $\rho{=}0.469$ (in-domain $0.379$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.090$), SJ $\rho{=}0.378$ (in-domain $0.360$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.018$), and FK $\rho{=}0.285$ (in-domain $0.267$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.018$).
The wider training schema subsumes CoNLL's narrower schema, so the model produces reasonable outputs even out-of-domain (greedy F1${=}0.522$), and structural signals benefit from the simpler target schema's reduced output ambiguity.

\paragraph{Narrower-to-wider schema transfer (excluded).}
The reverse direction is excluded from our conclusions due to catastrophic model failure, not signal failure.
The CoNLL-trained model recognizes only 4 news entity types (PER, ORG, LOC, MISC) and has no relation extraction capability; when applied to SciERC's 6 scientific entity types and 7 relation types, the model cannot produce meaningful structured outputs (greedy NER F1${=}0.009$, RE F1${=}0.001$).
Under this regime, most signals flip to negative or near-zero correlations (Table~\ref{tab:ood}); only VC retains weak positive correlation ($\rho{=}0.105$, $p{=}0.016$).
These negative correlations reflect the model systematically generating confident but incorrect outputs---a capability failure analogous to WNUT-17 (\S\ref{sec:qe_results}), not evidence against signal utility.

\paragraph{Asymmetry interpretation.}
The directional asymmetry is driven by schema coverage: wider$\to$narrower preserves signal utility because the SciERC model's 6-type schema subsumes CoNLL's 4 types, while narrower$\to$wider fails because the CoNLL model lacks the entity and relation types required by SciERC.
This extends the capability boundary identified on WNUT-17 to the domain-shift setting: confidence signals require sufficient model capability as a prerequisite, and results from the CoNLL$\to$SciERC direction should not be interpreted as evidence of signal degradation under domain shift.

1	\section{Experiments}
2	\label{sec:experiments}
3	
4	\subsection{Experimental Setup}
5	\label{sec:setup}
6	
7	\paragraph{Datasets.}
8	We evaluate on three English IE benchmarks spanning a difficulty gradient.
9	\textbf{SciERC} \cite{luan2018scierc} contains 551 test instances annotated for joint NER (6 types) and RE (7 types).
10	\textbf{CoNLL-2003} \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll} provides 3{,}453 test sentences with 4 entity types, where models achieve ${\approx}$91\% micro F1.
11	\textbf{WNUT-17} \cite{derczynski2017wnut} consists of 1{,}287 social media instances with emerging entities, used to probe method boundaries (52\% zero F1).
12	
13	\paragraph{Models and sampling.}
14	Both \textbf{Qwen3-8B} and \textbf{LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct} are fine-tuned with LoRA (rank$=$32, $\alpha{=}64$) for 5 epochs using LLaMA Factory \cite{zheng2024llamafactory} under identical training procedures, ensuring comparisons across the two model families (both at 8B scale) reflect model differences rather than training confounds.
15	We note a training confound for SciERC: Qwen3-8B's SciERC checkpoint was trained with \texttt{enable\_thinking=True} (LLaMA Factory 0.9.4 default), which prepends empty \texttt{<think>\textbackslash n</think>} blocks (4--5 tokens) to each training response and includes them in the loss computation; CoNLL-2003 and WNUT-17 checkpoints explicitly set \texttt{enable\_thinking=False}.
16	No reasoning content is present (the blocks are always empty), and constrained decoding at inference time enforces JSON-only output, so thinking tokens do not appear in generated samples.
17	This constitutes a minor train--test distribution mismatch for SciERC ($<$0.3\% of the 2048-token training window); CoNLL-2003 and WNUT-17 are unaffected.
18	We discuss implications in the Limitations section.
19	We draw $N{=}8$ samples at $T{=}1.0$ (primary; single seed, seed${=}42$), with $N{=}16$ for scaling experiments.\footnote{$N{=}16$ results for CoNLL (Qwen) and SciERC (LLaMA) are in Table~\ref{tab:robustness} (Appendix~\ref{app:robustness}); detailed $N$-scaling analysis in Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}. A 3-seed stability analysis ($\sigma{\leq}0.026$; Table~\ref{tab:multiseed}, Appendix~\ref{app:multiseed}) confirms that signal rankings are identical across seeds.}
20	Quality estimation uses Spearman $\rho$ and AUROC; downstream utility uses best-of-$N$ selection macro F1 (instance-averaged) with exact span matching (NER) and head-tail-label matching (RE).
21	Inference uses vLLM with constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided}.
22	
23	%% ============================================================
24	\subsection{Quality Estimation Results}
25	\label{sec:qe_results}
26	
27	\begin{table*}[t]
28	\centering
29	\small
30	\caption{Quality estimation across tasks and models (Spearman $\rho$ and AUROC; $N{=}8$, seed${=}42$). Best value per column in \textbf{bold}. SciERC evaluates joint NER (6 types) and RE (7 types, single benchmark---preliminary); CoNLL evaluates NER (4 types). $N{=}16$ results appear in Table~\ref{tab:robustness} (Appendix~\ref{app:robustness}).}
31	\label{tab:quality_estimation}
32	\begin{tabular}{ll cc cc cc cc}
33	\toprule
34	& & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{SciERC NER}} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{SciERC RE}} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{CoNLL (Qwen)}} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{CoNLL (LLaMA)}} \\
35	\cmidrule(lr){3-4} \cmidrule(lr){5-6} \cmidrule(lr){7-8} \cmidrule(lr){9-10}
36	Signal & Family & $\rho$ & AUC & $\rho$ & AUC & $\rho$ & AUC & $\rho$ & AUC \\
37	\midrule
38	VC & Structural & \textbf{.379} & .684 & \textbf{.350} & .694 & .424 & .789 & .426 & .709 \\
39	SJ  & Structural & .360 & .692 & .250 & .670 & .436 & .801 & \textbf{.431} & .704 \\
40	FK & Surface & .267 & .629 & .275 & .609 & .400 & .774 & .428 & .703 \\
41	EM  & Surface    & .295 & \textbf{.749} & .134 & \textbf{.706} & \textbf{.451} & \textbf{.816} & \textbf{.431} & .705 \\
42	LP     & Model      & .205 & .578 & .266 & .601 & .316 & .753 & .307 & \textbf{.761} \\

50	\caption{Quality estimation heatmap (Spearman $\rho$) across five signals and four configurations. Left: full evaluation set; right: conditional set (non-zero F1 instances). On the full set, structural signals dominate on SciERC NER while all signals converge on CoNLL. On the conditional set, EM emerges as the strongest signal on both NER ($\rho{=}0.360$) and RE ($\rho{=}0.417$), while LP RE collapses to near-zero ($\rho{=}0.011$).}
51	\label{fig:signal_heatmap}
52	\end{figure*}
53	
54	Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation} presents rank correlation ($\rho$) and AUROC for five confidence signals across tasks and models.
55	
56	\paragraph{Difficulty-dependent signal complementarity.}
57	On SciERC NER (complex schema, 6 types), structural signals lead: VC achieves $\rho{=}0.379$ and SJ $\rho{=}0.360$, both outperforming surface ($\rho{\leq}0.295$) and LP ($\rho{=}0.205$).
58	This advantage persists on RE (VC $\rho{=}0.350$; preliminary, single benchmark), though all signals weaken due to the 40\% zero-F1 floor effect.
59	VC and SJ show moderate instance-level correlation (NER: $\rho{=}0.659$; RE: $\rho{=}0.605$), indicating information overlap but not redundancy; their differential behavior across difficulty levels reflects the complementary granularity of entity-level frequency vs.\ span-level set overlap.
60	While the best $\rho{=}0.38$ (VC) explains approximately 14\% of F1 variance, the best AUROC reaches 0.749 (EM), indicating strong binary discriminative power for the quality/failure classification most relevant to practitioners in quality-aware routing.\footnote{Semantic entropy \cite{kuhn2023semantic} achieves comparable AUROC on discrete-answer QA; direct comparison is not meaningful due to different output spaces.}
61	Pairwise bootstrap CIs confirm the SJ advantage over LP ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.155$, CI excludes zero) but not over EM ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.065$, marginal under Bonferroni correction; Table~\ref{tab:bootstrap_signal_ci}, Appendix~\ref{app:bootstrap_signal}).
62	
63	\paragraph{$\rho$--AUROC dissociation.}
64	Signal choice depends on the intended use: on NER, EM leads AUROC (0.749) despite ranking third in $\rho$ (0.295), preferred for binary quality triage; structural signals ($\rho{\geq}0.36$) are better for fine-grained ranking.
65	On CoNLL with LLaMA, LP leads AUROC (0.761) yet trails in $\rho$ (0.307), confirming this pattern across datasets.
66	
67	\paragraph{Signal rankings shift with task difficulty.}
68	On CoNLL (greedy F1${\approx}$0.91), EM leads ($\rho{=}0.451$, AUROC${=}0.816$), surpassing SJ and VC.
69	When most samples are near-correct, binary agreement captures remaining variance more efficiently than set-level similarity.
70	This crossover---EM${>}$SJ on easy tasks vs.\ SJ${>}$EM on hard tasks---demonstrates difficulty-dependent complementarity rather than a uniform structural advantage, suggesting practitioners should match signal type to expected task difficulty.
71	Stability across the two model families (both 8B) is strong: SJ achieves $\rho{=}0.436$ (Qwen) vs.\ $0.431$ (LLaMA) on CoNLL ($\Delta{=}0.005$, within 3-seed $\sigma{\approx}0.007$).
72	On WNUT-17 ($N{=}16$), where 52\% of instances receive zero F1, full-set correlations are misleading: VC achieves $\rho{=}0.724$ (AUROC${=}0.913$), but this is entirely driven by the zero/non-zero boundary (conditional $\rho{=}0.038$, n.s.; Table~\ref{tab:wnut}).
73	LP exhibits strong \textit{negative} correlation ($\rho{=}{-}0.410$, AUROC${=}0.219$).
74	We hypothesize that this reversal reflects overconfidence on out-of-distribution inputs \citep{xiong2024llm}: the model assigns high log-probabilities to fluent but incorrect entity patterns (e.g., common noun phrases that resemble but do not match rare WNUT entity types), while producing lower scores for genuinely uncertain outputs where it correctly hedges.
75	On the conditional set, all signals collapse toward weak or non-significant correlations ($\rho{\leq}0.35$), with SJ achieving only $\rho{=}0.089$ ($p{=}0.020$) on the full set---suggesting a capability boundary beyond which consistency signals capture binary success/failure but not quality gradation.
76	
77	\paragraph{Conditional filtering.}
78	Filtering to non-zero F1 instances separates binary success detection (can the model extract \textit{anything}?) from quality gradation (among successful extractions, which are better?), but excludes the hardest instances where models fail completely---the conditional set is easier on average.
79	This reshuffles signal rankings (Figure~\ref{fig:signal_heatmap}, right).
80	EM emerges as the strongest conditional signal on both NER ($\rho{=}0.360$) and RE ($\rho{=}0.417$; preliminary), while VC and FK drop substantially (VC NER: $0.379{\to}0.300$; FK NER: $0.267{\to}0.176$).
81	LP RE collapses to $\rho{=}0.011$, confirming its full-set correlation was driven by zero/non-zero separation.
82	This creates a natural complementarity: VC and SJ are preferred on the full set, while EM provides the most precise ranking within the non-trivial subset (see Appendix~\ref{app:additional} for details).
83	A two-stage pipeline---using structural signals for quality-aware routing, then EM for within-batch ranking among non-trivial instances---could leverage each signal's regime of strength.
84
